subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 6-year-old boy develops a clusters of small blisters around his nose and mouth that rupture to form thick honey-colored crusts. Several other children in his daycare have similar lesions. He is afebrile and the lesions are confined to the superficial epidermis.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition and its most likely cause?

options.text: A highly contagious superficial epidermal infection with honey-colored crusting, usually due to S aureus or S pyogenes
An infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics with a sharply demarcated raised border
An acute painful spreading infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue
A walled-off collection of pus within the deeper layers of skin, almost always due to S aureus
A bullous eruption with large flaccid blisters caused by S aureus

explanation_correct: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial epidermal infection usually caused by S aureus or S pyogenes, characterized by honey-colored crusting. It is common in children and spreads readily in close-contact settings such as daycare. This boy's superficial honey-crusted lesions and daycare outbreak are classic. Bullous impetigo is a variant with bullae, usually from S aureus, but the description here is the non-bullous crusted form.

explanation_incorrect.B: Infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics with a well-demarcated raised border describes erysipelas, typically from S pyogenes, not honey-crusted impetigo.
explanation_incorrect.C: A painful spreading infection of deeper dermis and subcutis describes cellulitis, which lacks the superficial honey-colored crusting of impetigo.
explanation_incorrect.D: A walled-off pus collection in deeper skin describes an abscess, almost always from S aureus, not a superficial crusted eruption.
explanation_incorrect.E: Large flaccid bullae describe bullous impetigo, a variant not present here since this patient has honey-colored crusts rather than bullae.

educationalObjective: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial infection with honey-colored crusts, usually from S aureus or S pyogenes.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Skin infections: bacterial and viral

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 55-year-old man develops a bright red, warm, tender area on his lower leg after a minor cut. The lesion has a sharply defined, raised border that clearly separates infected from normal skin, and it is associated with fever and tender regional lymph nodes. There is no pus collection or crepitus.
question: Which of the following best identifies the anatomic level and likely cause of this infection?

options.text: Infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue with an ill-defined, spreading border
A walled-off collection of pus within the deeper layers of skin
A superficial epidermal infection with honey-colored crusting
Infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, usually by S pyogenes, with a well-defined raised border
A deep necrotizing infection with gas formation and crepitus

explanation_correct: Erysipelas is an infection involving the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, usually caused by S pyogenes. It presents with a well-defined, raised demarcation between infected and normal skin, along with fever and lymphangitis, matching this patient's sharply bordered plaque. By contrast, cellulitis involves the deeper dermis and subcutis with ill-defined spreading margins. The absence of crepitus or a pus collection excludes necrotizing fasciitis and abscess.

explanation_incorrect.A: Deeper dermis and subcutaneous infection with an ill-defined spreading border describes cellulitis, not the sharply demarcated raised lesion shown here.
explanation_incorrect.B: A walled-off pus collection describes an abscess, which would present as a fluctuant mass rather than a sharply bordered red plaque.
explanation_incorrect.C: A superficial epidermal infection with honey-colored crusting describes impetigo, not an upper dermal lymphatic infection with a raised border.
explanation_incorrect.E: A deep necrotizing infection with gas and crepitus describes necrotizing fasciitis, a surgical emergency not present here.

educationalObjective: Erysipelas infects upper dermis and superficial lymphatics (usually S pyogenes) with a sharply demarcated raised border, unlike deeper cellulitis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 60-year-old man with diabetes develops rapidly progressive swelling and discoloration of his left leg after a minor puncture wound. He is toxic-appearing and complains of excruciating pain that seems far worse than the examination findings suggest. Palpation reveals crepitus, and violaceous bullae are forming. Emergency imaging shows gas in the soft tissues.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.text: Uncomplicated cellulitis managed with oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up
Necrotizing fasciitis from anaerobic bacteria or S pyogenes, with methane and CO2 gas producing crepitus and violaceous bullae; a surgical emergency
Erysipelas from S pyogenes, managed with narrow-spectrum antibiotics
A simple abscess requiring only incision and drainage
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome from an exotoxin, managed with supportive care alone

explanation_correct: Necrotizing fasciitis is a deep tissue infection usually caused by anaerobic bacteria or S pyogenes. Pain out of proportion to examination findings, crepitus from methane and CO2 production, and violaceous bullae with skin necrosis are characteristic. It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics. This patient's rapid progression, gas on imaging, and out-of-proportion pain make it the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uncomplicated cellulitis is a painful but spreading superficial-to-deep infection that lacks crepitus, gas, violaceous bullae, and severe toxicity; it is not a surgical emergency.
explanation_incorrect.C: Erysipelas has a well-demarcated raised border and involves upper dermis and lymphatics, not gas-forming deep necrosis with pain out of proportion.
explanation_incorrect.D: A simple abscess is a walled-off pus collection without crepitus, gas in tissues, or rapidly progressive skin necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is an exotoxin-mediated superficial epidermal sloughing in newborns or renal insufficiency, not a gas-forming deep tissue infection.

educationalObjective: Necrotizing fasciitis (anaerobes/S pyogenes) causes pain out of proportion, crepitus from gas, and violaceous bullae; it requires emergent surgery.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 2-day-old newborn develops fever and a diffuse erythematous rash. Within hours the upper layers of epidermis slough off in sheets, leaving raw, denuded areas. Manual stroking of the skin causes epidermal separation. The mucous membranes are spared, and the denuded areas heal completely without scarring.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this condition and how it differs from toxic epidermal necrolysis?

options.text: A bacterial exotoxin destroys the epidermal-dermal junction, with prominent mucosal involvement and incomplete healing
Autoantibodies cause acantholysis of keratinocyte desmosomes throughout the epidermis
A bacterial exotoxin destroys keratinocyte attachments in the stratum granulosum only, with no mucosal involvement, a positive Nikolsky sign, and complete healing
A type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a contact allergen produces subcorneal pustules
A poxvirus infection produces umbilicated papules that ulcerate

explanation_correct: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by a staphylococcal exotoxin that destroys keratinocyte attachments in the stratum granulosum only. This produces superficial epidermal sloughing with a positive Nikolsky sign (epidermal separation on stroking), no mucosal involvement, and complete healing. It occurs classically in newborns and in children or adults with renal insufficiency. Toxic epidermal necrolysis, in contrast, destroys the epidermal-dermal junction and often involves mucosae.

explanation_incorrect.A: Destruction of the epidermal-dermal junction with mucosal involvement describes toxic epidermal necrolysis, not staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, which spares mucosae and heals completely.
explanation_incorrect.B: Autoantibody-mediated acantholysis of desmosomes is the mechanism of pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disease, not a bacterial exotoxin syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: A type IV contact allergen reaction describes allergic contact dermatitis, not an exotoxin-mediated superficial epidermal sloughing with Nikolsky sign.
explanation_incorrect.E: A poxvirus producing umbilicated papules describes molluscum contagiosum, not a diffuse exotoxin-mediated epidermal slough.

educationalObjective: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is an exotoxin destroying stratum granulosum only, with Nikolsky sign, no mucosal involvement, and complete healing.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 30-year-old man has recurrent painful grouped vesicles on his lower lip, especially during periods of stress. He has also had similar vesicular lesions on his finger after a dental procedure and a past episode of genital ulcers. The lesions are vesicles on an erythematous base that crust over.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this group of infections?

options.text: A poxvirus infection producing firm umbilicated papules
Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a dermatomal distribution
Low-risk HPV producing koilocytes and cauliflowerlike warts
Epstein-Barr virus producing white plaques on the lateral tongue
HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections including herpes labialis, herpes genitalis, and herpetic whitlow

explanation_correct: Herpes simplex virus infections (HSV-1 and HSV-2) can occur anywhere from mucosal surfaces to normal skin and include herpes labialis (cold sores), herpes genitalis, and herpetic whitlow (a painful infection of the finger). Recurrent painful vesicles on an erythematous base, triggered by stress, and the finger lesion after a dental procedure are characteristic. The other options describe unrelated viral infections with different morphologies.

explanation_incorrect.A: A poxvirus producing umbilicated papules describes molluscum contagiosum, not recurrent painful vesicles.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dermatomal reactivation of varicella-zoster virus describes zoster (shingles), a band-like vesicular eruption, not labialis, genitalis, or whitlow.
explanation_incorrect.C: Low-risk HPV produces warts with koilocytosis and condyloma acuminatum, not painful recurrent vesicles.
explanation_incorrect.D: Epstein-Barr virus causes hairy leukoplakia, painless white lateral tongue plaques, not vesicular skin lesions.

educationalObjective: HSV-1 and HSV-2 cause herpes labialis, genitalis, and herpetic whitlow, presenting as recurrent painful vesicles.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 7-year-old child has multiple small, firm, dome-shaped papules on the trunk and abdomen. Many of the lesions have a central umbilication (a small dimple). They are minimally symptomatic and have slowly increased in number over several months. No fever or systemic illness is present.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of these lesions?

options.text: Low-risk human papillomavirus producing koilocytes
A poxvirus producing umbilicated papules
Herpes simplex virus producing vesicles on an erythematous base
Malassezia species producing hypopigmented patches
Bartonella infection producing capillary papules with a neutrophilic infiltrate

explanation_correct: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and produces characteristic umbilicated papules. It is frequently seen in children, though it may also be sexually transmitted in adults. The small dome-shaped papules with central umbilication in this child are classic. The lesions are benign and often self-limited. The other options produce distinctly different morphology or histology.

explanation_incorrect.A: Low-risk HPV produces cauliflowerlike warts with koilocytes, not small umbilicated papules.
explanation_incorrect.C: Herpes simplex virus produces painful vesicles on an erythematous base, not firm umbilicated papules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Malassezia causes tinea versicolor with hypopigmented or pink patches and spaghetti-and-meatballs forms on KOH, not papules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis, benign capillary papules in AIDS with a neutrophilic infiltrate, not umbilicated papules in a healthy child.

educationalObjective: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus causing umbilicated papules, common in children and sexually transmissible in adults.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Skin infections: bacterial and viral

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 72-year-old man develops a painful, burning vesicular rash arranged in a band wrapping around the left side of his chest in a single dermatomal distribution. Decades earlier he had chickenpox, with lesions in various stages of vesicles and crusts. He is otherwise immunocompetent.
question: Which of the following best explains the relationship between his childhood and current illnesses?

options.text: A poxvirus causing umbilicated papules in children and reactivating in adults
Recurrent HSV-1 infection causing herpes labialis and herpetic whitlow
EBV-mediated hairy leukoplakia occurring with immunosuppression
Varicella-zoster virus causes varicella with crops of lesions in various stages, and zoster as reactivation in a dermatomal distribution
Low-risk HPV causing verrucae that disseminate along dermatomes

explanation_correct: Varicella-zoster virus causes two distinct illnesses. Varicella (chickenpox) presents with multiple crops of lesions in various stages from vesicles to crusts, as this patient had in childhood. Zoster (shingles) is reactivation of the latent virus in a dermatomal distribution, producing a painful band-like vesicular rash, as seen now. Unless disseminated, zoster remains confined to one or a few dermatomes. The other options describe different viruses and morphologies.

explanation_incorrect.A: A poxvirus causes molluscum contagiosum with umbilicated papules, not a dermatomal vesicular reactivation or chickenpox.
explanation_incorrect.B: Recurrent HSV-1 causes labialis or whitlow, not a dermatomal band, and does not cause varicella in childhood.
explanation_incorrect.C: EBV-mediated hairy leukoplakia produces painless white lateral tongue plaques in immunosuppressed patients, not vesicular dermatomal rashes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Low-risk HPV causes warts that do not follow dermatomes and are not a reactivation of a childhood exanthem.

educationalObjective: VZV causes varicella (lesions in various stages) and zoster (painful dermatomal reactivation).
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Skin infections: bacterial and viral

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 44-year-old man with HIV develops irregular, white, painless plaques on the lateral surface of his tongue. The plaques cannot be scraped off with a tongue depressor. He also has a history of an episode of thrush in which the white plaques were easily scrapable. His physician notes that a different white tongue lesion is considered precancerous.
question: Which of the following best identifies this lesion and distinguishes it from the other white tongue lesions mentioned?

options.text: EBV-mediated hairy leukoplakia: painless lateral tongue plaques that cannot be scraped off, seen in HIV and transplant patients
Candidal thrush: white plaques that are readily scrapable, leaving an erythematous base
HPV-associated condyloma acuminatum: cauliflowerlike papules with koilocytosis
HSV-related herpetic whitlow: painful vesicles on a finger
Leukoplakia: a precancerous white plaque that also cannot be scraped off

explanation_correct: Hairy leukoplakia is an EBV-mediated condition seen in patients living with HIV and organ transplant recipients. It produces irregular, white, painless plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off. This contrasts with candidal thrush, which is scrapable, and with leukoplakia, which is a precancerous lesion. This patient's HIV status, painless lateral tongue plaques, and inability to scrape them off make hairy leukoplakia the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Candidal thrush produces scrapable white plaques revealing an erythematous base, unlike the firmly adherent plaques described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: HPV-associated condyloma acuminatum produces cauliflowerlike warts with koilocytosis on the anus or genitals, not lateral tongue plaques.
explanation_incorrect.D: Herpetic whitlow is a painful HSV infection of the finger with vesicles, not a painless white tongue lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Leukoplakia is a precancerous white plaque, but it is a distinct entity; this patient's EBV-associated, HIV-related, non-scrapable lateral tongue lesion is hairy leukoplakia.

educationalObjective: Hairy leukoplakia is an EBV-driven, non-scrapable, painless lateral tongue plaque in HIV/transplant patients, unlike scrapable thrush or precancerous leukoplakia.
